claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The same CoCrFeNiTi state has favorable ductility and machinability.
Simple solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi exhibits only modest lattice distortion.
Simple solid-solution CoCrFeNiTi lacks second phases and short-range ordering that would provide additional dislocation obstacles.
Ordered regions or secondary phases can raise hardness or yield strength in high-entropy alloys.
A weakly ordered, more nearly single-phase state can provide lower yield strength and greater ductility than a strongly ordered or precipitate-strengthened state.
The absence of strong lattice distortion, ordering, and second-phase obstacles permits relatively easy dislocation glide, causing lower hardness and yield strength but greater plasticity.
Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti have sufficiently similar atomic sizes to produce relatively low lattice strain in CoCrFeNiTi.
Greater atomic-size mismatch and chemical heterogeneity impede dislocation motion through enhanced solid-solution and precipitation strengthening.
Replacing 2–10 at.% of Ti in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi with Al will increase lattice distortion.
Al substitution may promote short-range ordering or nanoscale precipitate formation in CoCrFeNiTi.
Increasing lattice distortion by controlled Al substitution should increase hardness and yield strength relative to unmodified CoCrFeNiTi.
The modified alloys may show moderately lower ductility than baseline CoCrFeNiTi.
Modified alloys should contain more nanoscale precipitates or ordered domains than the unmodified single-phase alloy.
Classical dislocation glide governs deformation in these alloys from ambient temperature to approximately 600 °C.
The controlled comparison will use baseline CoCrFeNiTi and Al-for-Ti substitution variants processed identically and tested at room temperature.
A statistically nonsignificant change in both hardness and yield strength after a verified increase in lattice distortion would falsify the proposed strengthening mechanism.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to isolate increased lattice distortion, but Al substitution is also expected to alter chemical identity and produce ordering or precipitates. Those simultaneous changes prevent the proposed experiment from isolating lattice distortion from ordering and precipitation strengthening.

The hypothesis permits lattice distortion, short-range order, or precipitates as alternative strengthening mediators, whereas the falsification rule can reject the hypothesis merely because ordered domains or precipitates fail to appear. Their absence would not by itself falsify strengthening through increased lattice distortion.
